newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Media mogul Black wants half of Australia's Fairfax.
newsitem.headline: Media mogul Black wants half of Australia's Fairfax.

text.p: Canadian media baron Conrad Black said on Wednesday he wanted to increase his stake in Australia's oldest newspaper group, John Fairfax Holdings Ltd, to 50 percent from 25 percent to create more stability for the group.
However, Black repeated he would sell out of Fairfax if there was no easing in the current media ownership rules, which he described as "anachronistic".

Black told shareholders at Fairfax's annual meeting that he had he had told Prime Minister John Howard on Tuesday in their first meeting since Howard won election in March that he would like to raise his stake in the newspaper group.

The media baron was asked by reporters after the meeting just how much he wanted to increase his stake to, if allowed. "Fifty percent," he said. His current stake is held through Toronto-based Hollinger International Inc.
The newspaper magnate has consistently sought a higher stake in Fairfax since leading a consortium in 1991 to buy Fairfax out of receivership in order to create stability and ward off any predators.
"There is an instability about the future for all Fairfax employees and all the Fairfax observers know that," Black said referring to regular takeover rumours about Fairfax.

Australia's richest man, Kerry Packer, has a 15 percent stake in Fairfax through his media empire Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd (PBL), while fellow media baron Rupert Murdoch owns five percent of Fairfax through his News Corp media group.

Packer has said previously he would like to own Fairfax, while Murdoch, who controls 66 percent of Australia's metropolitan newspaper circulation, has described Fairfax's classified advertising revenue as "rivers of gold".

Black, 52, said U.S. accounting rules effectively punished companies which had higher than 50 percent stakes in their associates. However, Black repeated that he would sell his Fairfax stake if he was not allowed to raise it further.

"If the road is truly blocked, then obviously we are going," Black said. "If we become satisfied that there is no chance of going beyond 25 percent we would go as soon as we could at what we consider to be a reasonable exit," he said.
Hollinger would not lodge any application for a higher stake until the government ended its study into media ownership and presented the new ownership rules, he said.
Under Australia's current media ownership rules, foreigners are prevented from owning more than 25 percent of a newspaper group or 15 percent of a television group.

The rules also prevent a newspaper group owner from holding more than 15 percent of a television station in the same city and vice-versa. "These things as they are now are very anachronistic," Black told reporters.
Although a sale of Hollinger's stake in Fairfax could not be ruled out, the suggested plan by PBL to merge with Fairfax was unlikely to succeed, Black said.
In August, PBL proposed a merger between PBL and Fairfax only if media ownership rules were liberalised.
PBL owns top-rating television broadcaster Nine Network.
PBL's merger proposal was unlikely to succeed while he (Black) was a shareholder. "He (Packer) would have quite a time getting that one through," Black said.
"I don't ever rule out anything, but I think that's fairly improbable. If Mr Packer wants to control Fairfax he's going to have to do it the old-fashioned way and pay for it."
"I know he's averse to doing that," Black said.
